entries.text: Use stopping smoking as your most powerful lever
Stopping smoking is one of the most effective steps you can take for your heart, blood vessels, lungs and energy. Your body begins to recover after only a short time.
Set a specific stop date within the next two weeks and seek support. Guidance significantly increases the chance of success.
Your risk of a heart attack and many other conditions decreases with every smoke-free week.
Manage high blood pressure well
You have known high blood pressure. Persistently high values strain the heart, blood vessels and kidneys, often without noticeable symptoms. Good control significantly reduces your risk.
Stay in contact with your healthcare professional, measure your blood pressure regularly and support your treatment with physical activity and a salt-conscious diet.
Well-controlled blood pressure substantially reduces the risk of heart attack, stroke and kidney damage.
Measure your blood pressure
You do not currently know your blood pressure. Because high blood pressure usually causes no symptoms, measuring it is the only way to detect it early.
Measure your blood pressure several times at rest over the next few weeks, either at many pharmacies or with a home monitor.
You can identify early whether action is needed and take targeted preventive steps.
Include your family history in preventive care
Cardiovascular disease, diabetes or hereditary conditions occur in your close family. This does not determine your future, but it is a good reason to know your baseline values.
Discuss your family history with a doctor when convenient and have baseline values such as blood pressure, blood glucose and blood lipids measured.
Knowing your risk allows you to start prevention earlier and target it more precisely.
Have your personal risk assessed
You have not yet had your personal risk of conditions such as cancer, high blood pressure or type 2 diabetes assessed. High blood pressure in particular often goes unnoticed for a long time.

Arrange a check-up when convenient and have baseline values such as blood pressure, blood glucose and blood lipids measured. Depending on your age and family history, consider other screening examinations as well.
Knowing your values makes prevention specific and shows where attention is particularly worthwhile.
Use alcohol reduction as an effective lever
Your alcohol consumption is in the higher range. Drinking less has several positive effects at once, including on sleep, blood pressure, weight and long-term cancer risk.
Set several alcohol-free days each week and try alcohol-free alternatives when the opportunity arises.
Even a reduction in alcohol improves sleep, energy and several health measures at the same time.
Break up long periods of sitting regularly

You sit for many hours on a typical day. Long periods of sitting are associated with adverse health effects. Both regular physical activity overall and breaking up longer periods of sitting are important.
Add a short movement break every 60 minutes: stand up, stretch and walk a few steps.
Regular mini-breaks improve circulation, concentration and wellbeing.
Build confidence in everyday movement
You feel unconfident during everyday movements. This feeling is an important early warning sign of an increased risk of falls, and it responds very well to training.

Include short balance and strength exercises two or three times a week, such as standing on one leg while brushing your teeth, getting up from a chair without using your hands, or doing a few supported squats.
Targeted balance, strength and mobility training substantially reduces the risk of falls and supports your independence.
Set deliberate limits on screen and social-media time
Social media noticeably affects your wellbeing or daily life. Deliberate boundaries give your mind and sleep a break.
Set fixed screen-free periods, such as the first hour after waking and the hour before bed, and switch off unnecessary notifications.
Less constant stimulation improves concentration, mood and sleep.
Learn about your family history
You currently know little about your family's medical history. This knowledge helps you approach preventive care more precisely.
When convenient, ask close relatives whether cardiovascular disease, diabetes or cancer occurred at a young age, and write down what you learn.
Knowing your family history helps you time examinations and prevention more appropriately.
Ease into physical activity
You are currently rather inactive. The good news is that starting brings the greatest health benefit, and every movement counts.
Start with two or three short walks of 10 to 15 minutes each week and increase gradually.
Even small, regular sessions noticeably improve energy, mood and heart health.
Build strength purposefully

Your answers about everyday strength, your strength training or an optional short test show potential to improve muscular strength or local muscular endurance. Strength supports resilience, bones and functional independence and becomes particularly important with increasing age.
Set aside two fixed sessions per week to build strength, for example with squats, suitable push-up variations and lunges. Choose a safe variation that you can perform with control.
Regular strength training can support muscular strength, everyday function and physical independence.
Build aerobic fitness step by step
You are already somewhat active, which is good to see. More aerobic activity further strengthens the heart, circulation and metabolism. Around 150 minutes per week is a useful guide.
Add one session per week or extend your existing sessions by 10 minutes each.
Regular aerobic activity improves fitness and energy and supports your long-term cardiovascular profile.
Train mobility and balance
Your answers or the single-leg stance test indicate an opportunity to train balance or mobility. Both support safe everyday movement and functional independence.
Include simple balance and mobility exercises twice a week, such as standing on one leg while brushing your teeth or doing a short mobility routine.
Targeted balance and mobility training can improve confidence in movement and help prevent falls, particularly at an older age.
Improve fitness for everyday activities

Climbing stairs is currently difficult for you. This everyday demand can often be improved with training. However, new or severe shortness of breath, chest discomfort, dizziness or light-headedness should first be assessed medically.

If there are no warning signs, choose a manageable everyday activity and increase it gradually. Stop if you experience chest discomfort, unusual shortness of breath, dizziness or light-headedness and have this assessed.
Better everyday fitness makes the day easier while also strengthening your heart and muscles.
Include protein sources regularly

Your answer shows that you currently include a clear source of protein in several meals or snacks rather infrequently. Strength training provides the stimulus for muscle adaptation, and protein provides the building blocks. This question assesses the routine, not your actual daily intake.
Start with two main meals per day. Include a clear source of protein in each, such as legumes, tofu, eggs, quark, yoghurt, fish or meat. Once this works reliably, add a third occasion.
Together with strength training, an appropriate total intake supports building and maintaining muscle. More protein is not automatically better.
Increase plant diversity
You currently eat relatively few different plant foods. Diversity supports a healthy gut microbiome and provides valuable fibre and plant compounds.
Aim to add a few new varieties each week, for example one additional type of vegetable, legume or wholegrain food per day.
Greater plant diversity benefits several aspects of health at once.
Reduce highly processed foods
Highly processed products often appear in your diet. They frequently provide a lot of energy, salt and sugar while offering little satiety.
Replace one highly processed product each day with a minimally processed alternative, such as nuts or fruit instead of snack foods.
Even small swaps improve nutrient density and satiety.
Reduce liquid calories
Sweetened drinks provide a lot of sugar without making you feel full and can adversely affect blood glucose and weight.
Gradually replace sugar-sweetened beverages with water, unsweetened tea or water flavoured with fruit.
Less liquid sugar noticeably reduces the burden on metabolism and weight.
Include more omega-3
Omega-3-rich foods currently appear infrequently in your diet. They support the heart, brain and regulation of inflammation.
Include oily fish such as salmon, herring or mackerel once or twice a week, or add linseeds or walnuts to your meals each day.
A better omega-3 supply supports cardiovascular health and wellbeing.
Make meals more filling
You do not reliably feel full for several hours after main meals. A balanced composition can help reduce the need for snacks and energy dips.
Combine protein, fibre from vegetables, legumes or wholegrains, and some healthy fat in every main meal.
Balanced meals can support satiety and slow the rise in blood glucose after eating.
Make more room for sleep

You currently get rather little sleep. Needs depend on age and individual factors: adults usually need at least seven hours, while adolescents generally need eight to ten hours. Sleep supports recovery, metabolism and mood.
Gradually move your bedtime 15 to 30 minutes earlier and keep it as consistent as possible.
A little more sleep improves energy, concentration and appetite regulation.
Improve sleep quality purposefully
Your sleep currently leaves you feeling poorly rested and affects your daily life. Changes to your environment and evening routine can often help.
Keep your bedroom dark, cool and quiet, and make the last hour before bed calm and screen-free. If the problems continue for several weeks, seek medical advice.
Better sleep supports energy, mood, the immune system and concentration.
Stabilise your sleep schedule
Irregular sleep times disrupt your body clock and make restorative sleep more difficult.
Get up at similar times whenever possible, including at weekends, and spend some time in daylight in the morning.
A regular schedule makes it easier to fall asleep and stay asleep.
Seek support – you do not have to carry this alone
Some of your answers suggest increased emotional strain. This can affect anyone and is not a sign of weakness. Accepting help is a strong step.

Talk to someone you trust and consider professional support. For English-language emotional support, call Heart2Heart on 0800 143 000 daily from 6 to 11 p.m. If there is immediate danger, call the emergency number 144.
Early support provides noticeable relief and opens up new options for action.
Actively balance stress
You currently feel noticeably under pressure or find it difficult to relax. Persistent tension affects sleep, the heart, metabolism and mood.
Plan one short, deliberate break each day: take a few deep breaths, go for a walk or spend a few minutes away from screens.
Regular mini-breaks reduce tension and strengthen resilience.
Strengthen social connections
Supportive relationships are among the strongest protective factors for health. You currently feel less connected or supported.
Make a deliberate effort to contact someone who is good for you this week. A phone call or short message is enough to begin.
Greater connection has a positive effect on mood, stress and physical health.
Establish a small recovery routine
Recharging regularly helps you process stress more effectively. You currently set aside little deliberate time for this.
Choose an activity that feels good, such as movement, nature, music or a hobby, and reserve two fixed time slots for it this week.
Deliberate recovery strengthens your mental resilience in daily life.
Strengthen purpose and confidence
A sense of purpose in daily life and a confident outlook are important emotional resources. You currently experience both less strongly.
Consider which activity or connection gives you a sense of purpose and deliberately plan some of it this week.
A stronger sense of purpose and small successes support confidence and emotional health.
Have a cardiovascular screening check
Several factors together increase your cardiovascular risk. For you, these are: {{riskFactors}}. A medical check makes your personal risk more tangible and helps prioritise the next steps.
Manage high blood pressure well
Your known high blood pressure is your most important controllable risk factor. Measure it regularly and follow your treatment consistently.
Measure your blood pressure
You do not know your blood pressure. Because high blood pressure usually causes no symptoms, measuring it is the only way to detect it early.
Take steps to stop smoking – your single biggest lever
Stopping smoking is one of the most powerful controllable health levers. After about one year, the risk of coronary heart disease is approximately half that of someone who continues to smoke.
Reduce alcohol consumption

Your answers indicate frequent alcohol consumption. Both frequency and quantity, including heavy drinking on individual occasions, affect health risk. Overall, the less alcohol you drink, the lower the risk.
Train your balance and prevent falls
Feeling unconfident during everyday movements is an early warning sign. Targeted balance and strength training substantially reduces the risk of falls.
Break up sitting time regularly
Your answers indicate a long daily sitting time. Regular physical activity reduces overall risk, while repeatedly breaking up longer periods of sitting is a practical additional starting point.
Clarify your family medical history
Knowing your family history helps target preventive care. A conversation with your family is the simplest first step.
Set deliberate limits on social-media time
You spend more time online than you would like. Fixed screen-free periods help you regain control.
Build aerobic fitness step by step (goal: 150 min/week)

You are not very active and become short of breath when climbing stairs. If the shortness of breath is new, unusual or severe, have it assessed medically first. Otherwise, short and manageable walks can be a suitable starting point.
Aerobic fitness is an important part of cardiovascular health and everyday performance. Start with manageable walks and increase gradually.
Start strength training twice a week
From the age of 50, the body loses muscle each year without training. Strength exercise twice a week helps maintain strength, stability and independence.
Your muscles support metabolism and stability. Even two short sessions per week, including body-weight exercises, make a difference.
Train mobility and balance purposefully
Getting up from the floor is difficult for you. Exercises for leg strength, mobility and balance can train this functional ability directly.
Add more movement to daily life
Take the stairs instead of the lift, get off one stop earlier or add short walking breaks. Everyday movement adds up faster than you might think.
Replace sugary drinks with water or unsweetened options
Sugar-sweetened beverages are usually much less filling than solid foods. Replacing them with water or unsweetened options is therefore a manageable nutrition lever.
Gradually replace highly processed foods with fresh options
Highly processed products provide a lot of sugar, salt and less favourable fats. Every meal you replace counts, and perfection is not necessary.
Include protein sources regularly

Regular protein sources can support the maintenance of muscle mass and function together with strength training. The appropriate amount depends on body weight, training, energy intake and health status. Age alone is not a reason to aim for 2.0 g/kg/day.

Regular protein sources are a useful nutrition routine. This answer cannot show whether your personal daily intake is appropriate; relevant factors include body weight, strength training, energy intake and health status.
Gradually increase plant diversity
Diversity feeds your gut microbiome. Spices, herbs, nuts and seeds all count and make it easy to get started.
Plan a regular omega-3 source (oily fish or algal oil)
Oily fish provides the omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA. Two portions of fish per week align with common dietary recommendations. Supplements should not automatically be considered equivalent.
Discuss persistent hunger with a healthcare professional
If meals rarely leave you feeling full, it is worth looking at their composition and other possible causes. This can often be addressed effectively.
Seek medical advice for persistent exhaustion
You sleep long enough but are severely affected. This can have physical causes and should be assessed by a doctor.
Extend your sleep window to 7–9 hours
Insufficient sleep affects concentration, metabolism and the immune system. Move your bedtime earlier in small 15-minute steps.
Put screens away earlier in the evening
Frequent social-media use and restless sleep occur together in your answers. A calmer, screen-free period in the evening can help you see whether it makes it easier to switch off.
Establish fixed sleep and wake times
Your body clock thrives on regularity. A consistent wake time, including at weekends, is particularly helpful for stabilising sleep.
Build an evening routine for better sleep
Consistent rituals, dimmed light and a cool bedroom often improve sleep quality within just a few weeks.
Accept support – talk to a professional
Your answers indicate noticeable strain. Seeking support is a sign of strength, and it helps.
Schedule fixed periods of recovery in daily life
Recovery rarely happens by itself. Schedule small, fixed moments of calm as you would an appointment with yourself.
Build stress-management skills purposefully
Coping with pressure is a skill you can learn. Breathing exercises, short breaks and clear priorities are effective first tools.
Actively maintain social connections
Connection is one of the strongest protective factors for health. A small first step is to contact one person this week.
Smoke-free
You do not smoke, which is the single most important protective factor for your heart, blood vessels and lungs.
Successfully stopped smoking
You have stopped smoking, and your risk has continued to fall year by year ever since.
WHO physical-activity target achieved
Your weekly aerobic activity is within the recommended range, protecting your heart, metabolism and mental health.
Regular strength training
With at least two strength sessions per week, you meet the WHO recommendation and maintain muscle and stability.
Consistent, sufficient sleep
Sufficient sleep duration, good quality and a regular schedule support recovery. How much sleep is sufficient depends in part on age.
Low intake of sugar and highly processed foods
You rarely choose sugary drinks or highly processed products, one of the most effective nutrition habits.
Emotional resilience
You keep a clear overview in difficult situations and find ways to cope, which is a dependable resource.
Moderate approach to alcohol
You never or rarely drink alcohol, keeping your alcohol-related health burden low.
Wide variety of plant foods
Your varied selection of plant foods contributes to a diverse intake of fibre and micronutrients.
Purpose and joy in daily life
You experience your life as meaningful and regularly find moments of joy, a strong protective factor for mental health.
Restorative sleep
Overall, you sleep well, providing a foundation that benefits concentration, mood and recovery every day.
Fit for everyday life
Getting up, climbing stairs and carrying things: you manage these basic functional abilities without difficulty.
Strong social network
You feel accepted and included. Social connection is one of the strongest known protective factors.
Steady on your feet
You feel very confident during everyday movements, which at your age is valuable protection against falls.
Preventive care up to date and family risks known
You know your personal risk and family history, providing the best foundation for targeted prevention.
Protein sources included regularly
On most days, you include a source of protein in several meals or snacks. This is a good routine, but the answer does not show whether your personal daily amount is already appropriate.
{{dimensionTitle}} is your most stable area
Even if several things currently need attention, this is your most solid foundation and gives you something to build on.
Many aspects of your circumstances and habits already support your health. Targeted everyday decisions and regular preventive care can strengthen this area further.
You already include physical activity in daily life. A balanced mix of aerobic activity, strength and mobility can strengthen this area further.
Several of your nutrition habits are already beneficial. Small, practical changes can improve the quality further.
Several aspects of your sleep already support recovery. Small changes can further improve its quality or regularity.
You have mental resources. Regular breaks, relationships and helpful routines can strengthen them further.
Your circumstances and habits clearly support your health. Keep going, and use regular preventive care to maintain this good position.
You are pleasingly active. Continue to aim for a mix of aerobic activity, strength and mobility.
Your nutrition provides a good foundation. Enjoy staying on track.
Your sleep restores you well, providing a valuable foundation for everything else.
You have noticeable mental resources. Continue to nurture breaks, relationships and activities that are good for you.
Arrange a cardiovascular screening check
Several of your answers suggest that your cardiovascular risk should be assessed by a doctor: {{riskFactors}}. Current measurements can be taken and suitable next steps agreed together.
You receive current measurements and can clarify with a healthcare professional which next steps suit your risk profile.
Arrange an appointment soon to have your cardiovascular risk assessed using your blood pressure, blood lipids and blood glucose.
Arrange an appointment soon to have your blood pressure, blood lipids and blood glucose assessed, and mention your family history.

Arrange an appointment soon to have your blood pressure, blood lipids and blood glucose assessed. Continue your prescribed treatment as agreed and discuss an appropriate measurement schedule with the healthcare professional treating you.

Arrange an appointment soon to have your blood pressure, blood lipids and blood glucose assessed, and mention your family history. Continue your prescribed treatment as agreed and discuss an appropriate measurement schedule with the healthcare professional treating you.
At your next appointment, specifically discuss your cardiovascular risk and have your blood pressure, blood lipids and blood glucose measured again.
At your next appointment, specifically discuss your cardiovascular risk and family history and have your blood pressure, blood lipids and blood glucose measured again.

At your next appointment, specifically discuss your cardiovascular risk and have your blood pressure, blood lipids and blood glucose measured again. Until then, measure your blood pressure regularly and continue your current treatment consistently.

At your next appointment, specifically discuss your cardiovascular risk and family history and have your blood pressure, blood lipids and blood glucose measured again. Until then, measure your blood pressure regularly and continue your current treatment consistently.
Seek medical advice for severe sleep-related impairment
Your sleep severely affects your daily life. If this continues, possible physical or psychological causes should be assessed by a doctor.
Arrange an appointment with your GP and explain how long your sleep has been affecting daily life and in what ways, such as your energy, concentration, mood or social activities.
You gain clarity about possible causes and can decide on suitable next steps.
Put screens away earlier in the evening
Frequent social-media use and restless sleep occur together in your answers. Try a calmer, screen-free period in the evening to see whether it helps you switch off.
Try a fixed screen-free period before going to bed. Charging your phone out of reach or outside the bedroom can make this easier.
A calmer evening routine may make it easier to switch off and support sleep quality, while also giving you back screen-free time.
This week
Weeks 2–3
Week 4

Arrange an appointment and prepare specifically for the examination. In addition to blood pressure and blood glucose, ask for a lipid profile and specifically ask about ApoB (apolipoprotein B) and Lp(a) (lipoprotein(a)). Note in advance which relatives had cardiovascular disease and at what age, as this often materially changes the medical assessment.

Understand what the values mean. ApoB reflects the number of atherogenic particles, while LDL cholesterol measures their cholesterol content, and the two values can differ. Lp(a) is largely determined by genetics and is barely influenced by lifestyle. Measuring it once in adulthood is usually sufficient; a healthcare professional will determine any exceptions.

Set and record a follow-up schedule. The Swiss Heart Foundation recommends regular blood-lipid checks from the age of 40. An earlier measurement may be useful if you have a family history. Lp(a) is generally measured only once in adulthood; a healthcare professional will determine any exceptions. Deposits in blood vessels develop over years, so assessing risk early is worthwhile.

Set and record a follow-up schedule. The Swiss Heart Foundation recommends having blood lipids checked at least every five years from the age of 40 and blood glucose from the age of 45. Lp(a) is generally measured only once in adulthood; a healthcare professional will determine any exceptions. If you have an elevated risk or are receiving treatment, agree the intervals with your healthcare professional.

Set a specific stop date within the next 14 days and seek support. The national stop-smoking helpline 0848 000 181 provides free advice (Mon–Fri, 11 a.m.–7 p.m.; also online or by video). Ask a pharmacy or medical practice about nicotine replacement or medication. Combining advice and medication multiplies the chance of success compared with trying alone.

Relapse is common with dependence and does not mean failure. What matters is starting the next attempt. Write down your three strongest triggers, such as coffee, stress or the end of the working day, and define a specific alternative action for each. Irritation of the airways begins to ease after only a few days, and circulation and lung function improve noticeably after a few months.

Keep the gains over time in mind. After about one year, the risk of coronary heart disease is approximately half that of someone who continues to smoke; after ten years, the risk of lung cancer is about half. After around 15 years, the risk of coronary heart disease approaches that of someone who has never smoked. Record what has already changed for you, such as taste, fitness or money.

Measure your blood pressure while seated in the morning and evening on three days, after resting for five minutes, and record the values. The average over several days matters, not individual readings. This provides a reliable picture for your next consultation.

Two levers have proven effects: salt, most of which comes from ready-made products, bread, cheese and processed meat rather than the salt shaker, and aerobic activity on most days of the week. Reducing alcohol also helps. Implement one of these consistently instead of approaching all of them half-heartedly.

Take your series of measurements to your next appointment and clarify two questions: Have I reached my target value, and have my blood lipids, including ApoB, and Lp(a) ever been measured? High blood pressure and elevated blood lipids have a disproportionately large combined effect on blood vessels, so both factors should be considered together.

Measure your blood pressure at a pharmacy, with a home monitor or at a medical practice. As a rough guide, values from around 140/90 mmHg in a clinical measurement may require treatment, but the assessment belongs in medical hands.
Repeat the measurement on another two or three days. High blood pressure typically causes no symptoms, so measuring it is the only way to detect it early. One elevated value alone is not a diagnosis.

If the values are repeatedly elevated, arrange an appointment and have a lipid profile measured at the same time. If they are normal, schedule another check in one to two years. Preventive care works only when it becomes a routine rather than remaining a one-off action.

Walk briskly for 10–15 minutes three times. Use the talk test to find the right intensity: you can still hold a conversation but can no longer sing. Fixed calendar appointments are more effective than good intentions.

If you tolerate brisk walking well and without symptoms, add short, slightly more intense intervals once a week. Walk briskly uphill for 1–3 minutes, recover fully and repeat once or twice. These stimuli can complement your base training. If you have known heart disease, chest pain, unusual shortness of breath, dizziness or light-headedness, seek medical advice first.

Work towards the goal of 150 minutes of moderate-intensity activity per week (WHO), or 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity activity, with combinations also possible. Studies show a strong association between cardiorespiratory fitness, health and life expectancy. For people who have previously been less active, every additional amount of manageable movement therefore counts.
Schedule two fixed sessions of 25–30 minutes at an easy pace. Use the talk test: conversation is possible, singing is not. This calm base intensity builds the foundation and may feel easy.

If you tolerate the base training well and without symptoms, you can add one more intense session per week. After an easy warm-up, do 4–6 × 1 minute noticeably faster, with 2 easy minutes between intervals. Interval training can improve maximal oxygen uptake (VO₂max). Stop and seek medical assessment if you experience chest pain, unusual shortness of breath, dizziness or light-headedness.

Review your progress: do you reach 150 minutes of moderate-intensity or 75 minutes of vigorous-intensity activity per week? Increase duration or intensity, never both at the same time. A simple progress check is to notice how climbing two flights of stairs feels now.

Do two 20-minute body-weight sessions with squats, push-ups, including wall or knee variations, and lunges, for 2–3 sets each. The last two repetitions should feel clearly challenging; that is where the training stimulus occurs.

You already train on one day. Add a fixed second session each week. Do 20 minutes of body-weight exercises per session: squats, push-ups, including wall or knee variations, and lunges, for 2–3 sets each. The last two repetitions should feel clearly challenging; that is where the stimulus occurs.

You already train regularly. For the next four weeks, choose two exercises that are easy to control and suit your test result, and document the sets, repetitions and variation used. Progress only when you can perform them with good technique and without pain.

Increase the resistance, not just the number of repetitions, by moving more slowly, shortening rests or adding weight. Muscle mass and strength tend to decrease with age without a regular training stimulus; strength training can maintain and improve both, even at an older age.

Progress carefully by moving more slowly, shortening rests or adding resistance. With increasing age, strength and muscle mass become particularly important for preventing falls and maintaining independence. Strength and muscular function can be improved purposefully even at an older age.

Make twice a week for all major muscle groups, the WHO recommendation, a fixed appointment. Check your progress without equipment: how do two full shopping bags feel, and how easily can you get up from the floor?

Less than 5 hours noticeably affects concentration and health, so every additional half hour is worthwhile. Move your bedtime earlier in 15-minute steps, as abrupt changes often fail. Set an alarm for going to bed, not just for getting up.
Move your bedtime earlier in 15-minute steps, as abrupt changes often fail. Set an alarm for going to bed, not just for getting up.
Adults are regularly advised to get at least seven hours of sleep. Try a 15-minute earlier bedtime for one week and observe your energy and concentration during the day.

Above all, keep your wake time as consistent as possible, including at weekends. People metabolise caffeine at different rates, and it can still affect sleep hours later. Alcohol may make you feel sleepy, but it often fragments sleep and particularly reduces REM sleep.

Assess the result during the day, not at night: do you wake refreshed and avoid an afternoon slump? Most adults need 7–9 hours. If tiredness persists despite sufficient sleep, seek medical advice. Possible causes include sleep apnoea, iron deficiency or thyroid abnormalities.
Set a wake time that is as consistent as possible, including at weekends. Seek daylight as soon as possible after getting up, ideally outdoors, as morning light helps align your body clock.

Reduce large differences between workdays and days off. Strongly varying sleep times are known as “social jet lag” and are associated in studies with adverse sleep and metabolic characteristics. Choose a regular wake time that is as practical as possible in daily life.

Establish a short and consistent evening sequence, such as dimming the lights, airing the room and reading. The repetition matters more than the content: the body learns the signal and begins preparing for sleep.
Replace your first daily sugary drink with water or an unsweetened option. Depending on the product, half a litre of soft drink can contain around 50 g of sugar while providing little satiety.

Pure fruit juice also counts. Without the fibre of the whole fruit, what remains is mainly sugar. Make the healthier drink your default: place a water bottle visibly on the table and stop keeping sweetened drinks in stock.

Review your progress: on how many days did you manage without one? The effect works in two ways: fewer calories and more stable blood-glucose curves, which reduces cravings. Allow deliberate exceptions rather than prohibitions; it is the usual pattern that matters.

Take the first step by speaking with your GP, which is the usual and straightforward route into psychological support. For free and anonymous English-language emotional support, call Heart2Heart on 0800 143 000 daily from 6 to 11 p.m. If there is immediate danger, call 144.

Until the appointment, spend two minutes each day writing down what was difficult and what felt good. This may sound simple, but it creates distance and gives you specific material for the conversation instead of having to reconstruct everything in the moment. Also tell someone you trust how you are feeling.

The goal here is to keep going, not to perform. Emotional strain is treatable, and early support significantly shortens its course. Keep the appointment you arranged, even if you feel better in the meantime.
Twice a day, stand on one leg for 20–30 seconds per side while supported at the kitchen counter, for example while brushing your teeth. Also get up from a chair five times without using your hands.

Make it gradually more difficult: support yourself with only one finger and then without support, or slowly turn your head left and right. This works because balance is not a talent but a trainable interaction between muscles, joint-position sense and the inner ear, and it can improve measurably within a few weeks.

Add leg-strength exercises such as squats and stair climbing. Strength and balance together have been shown to reduce the risk of falls more than either measure alone. Also check for trip hazards at home, such as loose rugs, poor lighting and cables.

Arrange a check-up. Ask for blood pressure, blood glucose and a lipid profile. Ask whether ApoB provides additional information for your risk profile and whether Lp(a) has already been measured once. Many risk factors cause no symptoms for a long time, so current values provide a reliable basis for discussion.
Record your values and ask for your personal risk to be explained. A baseline value measured once makes every later change visible and makes prevention specific.
Record when the next check is appropriate, usually every 1–3 years depending on values and age, and schedule it. Preventive care works only when it becomes routine.

Gather information about which close relatives, including parents and siblings, developed which conditions and when. Particularly relevant: men before the age of 55 and women before the age of 65. This information often shifts the useful starting point for preventive care several years earlier.

Arrange an appointment and take this family history with you. Have baseline values measured, including blood pressure, blood glucose and blood lipids including ApoB/Lp(a), and have your risk assessed.
Clarify whether and when early-detection examinations are appropriate for you, and set the next follow-up appointment. A family history is not destiny; it is advance information if you use it.

Include two mini-exercises each day: stand on one leg in a safe environment with a stable support within reach, and get up from a chair five times with control and without using your hands. Stop if you experience pain or dizziness.

Add a short mobility routine for your hips, shoulders and spine twice a week. Progress the balance exercise gradually, for example by using less support or placing your feet slightly closer together, while still keeping a safe support within reach.

Make the exercises a fixed habit, ideally linked to something you already do, such as brushing your teeth or taking a coffee break. Balance and mobility are maintained only when they are challenged regularly.

First check for warning signs. If you experience new or severe shortness of breath, chest discomfort, dizziness or light-headedness, seek a medical assessment. Otherwise, choose a manageable everyday activity, such as a short flight of stairs or walking one public-transport stop, and increase gradually.
If the activity remains symptom-free, increase carefully: walk a little longer or add another short flight of stairs, then recover. This builds your everyday fitness step by step.
Make the active option your default choice. Check your progress without equipment: does climbing stairs already feel easier? That is how you notice progress in daily life.

Plan one or two fixed “fish days” per week with oily fish such as salmon, herring, mackerel or sardines. For a vegetarian or vegan option, algal oil provides omega-3 that the body can use directly, unlike the precursor in linseed oil.

Add a portion of ground linseeds, chia seeds or walnuts to your meals each day. Omega-3 has an anti-inflammatory effect and supports the heart and brain. The body does not produce it itself, so regular intake matters.
Make the fish days part of a fixed weekly routine and always keep a plant-based omega-3 source within easy reach. Regularity matters more than quantity.

Include protein, fibre-rich foods such as vegetables, legumes or wholegrains, and a suitable source of fat in every main meal. This combination can support satiety and slow the rise in blood glucose after the meal.

With suitable meals, try eating vegetables or salad and a source of protein before the carbohydrate-rich components. This order can slow the rise in blood glucose. Above all, observe which composition feels pleasant and keeps you full for long enough.
Make the filling combinations your standard recipes. If constant hunger persists despite a good composition, it is worth speaking with a nutrition professional, as there may be other causes.
Deliberately schedule an activity that gives you purpose or joy, however small it may seem. Purpose rarely appears by itself; it is created, often in very ordinary moments.
Try a simple gratitude exercise: each evening, write down three things that went well that day. This has been shown to direct attention towards the positive and supports a more confident outlook.

Make what is good for you a fixed part of your week, whether a connection, activity or commitment. If a loss of purpose or motivation persists, it is a good reason to seek support, which is a sign of strength.

Schedule three fixed alcohol-free days in your calendar. Choose specific weekdays rather than simply intending to drink less. On days when you drink alcohol, have a glass of water between alcoholic drinks.

Try appealing alcohol-free alternatives, such as alcohol-free beer, spritzers or mocktails, in situations where you would otherwise reach for a drink automatically. It is important to know that there is no amount that is “safe” for health, and every reduction counts.
Review which occasions you managed well without alcohol and keep the alcohol-free days as a fixed habit.
For example, use an hourly reminder to stand up, stretch or walk a few steps. Both total sitting time and long uninterrupted periods of sitting are relevant, and every additional movement counts.

Link movement to existing habits: make phone calls while standing, take the stairs instead of the lift or go for a short walk after lunch. Movement after a meal can slow the rise in blood glucose. Check whether you can use a standing workstation for part of the time.
Make short movement breaks a habit. Choose a schedule that works in daily life and regularly breaks up long uninterrupted periods of sitting.
Introduce two screen-free periods: the first hour after waking and the last hour before sleep. Charge your phone outside the bedroom overnight.

Deliberately increase the barrier instead of relying on willpower. Remove the two most time-consuming apps from the home screen, switch off push notifications and, if useful, set a time limit. Finding it difficult to disengage is a result of product design, not a lack of willpower.
Deliberately replace the time you have gained with something that is good for you, such as movement, connection or a hobby. This creates a benefit rather than a sense of deprivation.

Ask close relatives, including parents and siblings, whether cardiovascular disease, diabetes or cancer occurred at a young age. Particularly relevant are men before the age of 55 and women before the age of 65.

Write down the most important information: who, which condition and at what age. A family history is not destiny but useful information, and it often shifts the appropriate start of preventive care several years earlier.
Take the notes to your next medical appointment. This allows your healthcare professional to tailor preventive care and any early detection to your profile.
On two typical days, mark which meals already include a clear source of protein. First add legumes, tofu, eggs, quark, yoghurt, fish or meat to two main meals per day.

If possible, expand the routine to three meals or snacks with a clear source of protein. The question does not calculate a personal gram target. If you have kidney disease or a medically prescribed diet, discuss the appropriate amount with a healthcare professional.

If you are a healthy adult who regularly does strength training, around 1.4–1.6 g/kg/day is a practical guide. In the meta-analysis, the average additional benefits for building lean mass levelled off markedly from around 1.6 g/kg/day. Up to around 2.0 g/kg/day may be appropriate on an individual basis during very high training loads or a deliberate energy deficit. Most people do not need this, and age alone is not a reason to aim for it. If you have kidney disease or a medically prescribed diet, seek professional advice first.

On three typical days, check whether the planned protein sources have become practical in daily life. If an exact g/kg target is relevant for your training or diet, have it assessed for your situation. Protein powder is not automatically necessary.
Aim to add two or three new plant varieties. Spices, herbs, nuts and seeds all count, so getting started is easier than many people think.

A guide is around 30 different plant foods per week. Diversity feeds the gut microbiome, which in turn influences the immune system, metabolism and even mood. One practical trick is to try one new variety with each shop.
Establish fixed “diversity anchors”, such as a handful of mixed nuts or seeds each day and vegetables that vary each week, so variety becomes effortless.

Replace one highly processed meal or snack per day with something fresh, such as fruit, nuts, yoghurt or home-cooked food. A rule of thumb is that more than five ingredients or names that are difficult to pronounce often indicate a highly processed product.

Cook a simple fresh meal two or three times a week and deliberately prepare a little extra for lunch the next day. This automatically reduces reliance on ready-made food. The goal is not perfection but a lower proportion.
Make fresh basic ingredients standard supplies at home. When shopping, focus mainly on the perimeter of the shop for fresh foods rather than the aisles for processed products.
Optimise your bedroom: dark, cool (around 18 °C) and quiet. Introduce a calm final hour without screens; dimmed light signals to the body that sleep is approaching.

Keep caffeine to the first half of the day where possible. Metabolism varies between people, and late caffeine can still affect sleep hours later. Alcohol may make you feel sleepy, but it often fragments sleep and particularly reduces REM sleep. Regular wake and bedtimes give sleep structure.
Keep the routine consistent. If the problems continue for several weeks despite good habits, seek medical advice, as there may be a treatable cause.
Schedule two fixed 10-minute breaks per day in your calendar, without screens. Recovery does not simply happen in spare time; it must be planned like an appointment.

Add a short technique shown to reduce the stress response: a few minutes of deliberate, slow breathing, such as 4 seconds in and 6 seconds out, or a walk in nature. Regularity matters more than duration.
Make the most effective break a fixed daily ritual. If you notice that the strain remains high over time, seek additional support. This is a sign of strength.
Actively contact one person who is good for you and arrange something specific, with a day and time rather than a vague intention to meet again.
Create a recurring connection, such as a fixed walk, phone call or shared meal. Social connection is one of the strongest known protective factors for health and life expectancy.
Establish at least one regular social appointment each week. A club, course or volunteer role can also create reliable encounters.
Schedule one fixed, small period of recovery each day, like an appointment with yourself: 10 minutes without a screen, a walk, tea or music. Recovery rarely happens by itself.
Observe what genuinely gives you energy rather than merely distracting you, and include more of it. Short, regular moments are more effective than rare, long breaks.
Make the most effective period of recovery a fixed, non-negotiable daily ritual.

Arrange an appointment with your GP and note in advance how long the tiredness has lasted, how severely it affects daily life and whether there are accompanying symptoms such as snoring, pauses in breathing or headaches.

Until the appointment, keep a short sleep and energy diary, including bedtimes, waking and daytime energy. Common and treatable causes include sleep apnoea, iron deficiency or thyroid abnormalities, which can be assessed specifically.
Discuss the results and recommended next steps. Keep going until the cause is found. Persistent exhaustion is not something you simply have to accept.
Introduce a fixed screen-free hour before bed and charge your phone outside the bedroom. The greatest effect comes when the device is not within reach in the first place.

Replace evening scrolling with a calm routine, such as reading, stretching or music. Increase the barrier to the most time-consuming apps by removing them from the home screen and switching off notifications. Finding it difficult to disengage is a result of product design, not a lack of willpower.
Make the screen-free evening hour a matter of course. Notice how your time to fall asleep and sleep quality have changed.
Increased emotional strain
Persistent strain has also been shown to change physical processes, including sleep, blood pressure and the immune system. It is treatable, and support works faster when sought early.
A professional can distinguish temporary strain from a condition that needs treatment and identify suitable support.

A GP practice can be a first point of contact and refer you to suitable psychological or psychiatric support if necessary. Seeking support early can help assess the strain and begin appropriate steps.
Known high blood pressure
High blood pressure and adverse blood lipids both contribute to cardiovascular risk. Well-controlled blood pressure reduces this risk, even if the change is often not directly noticeable.
Your target value, medication and, something often overlooked, whether your blood lipids including ApoB and your Lp(a) have ever been measured.

One detail for the medical consultation: depending on your risk profile, ApoB may provide additional information beyond the lipid profile. Lp(a) should generally be measured at least once in adulthood.
Blood pressure unknown
High blood pressure typically causes no symptoms. You can have it for years without noticing, so measuring it is the only way to detect it.
Whether values are repeatedly elevated and whether other risk factors are present.
Family history
A family history is not destiny but useful information. It moves the appropriate starting point for preventive care earlier, often by years.
Which relatives developed which conditions and at what age; onset before age 55 in men or before age 65 in women is particularly relevant; and whether genetic assessment is appropriate.
If you are known to have elevated Lp(a), a healthcare professional can discuss with you whether testing your parents, siblings or children is appropriate. Lp(a) is largely genetically determined.
Personal risk never assessed
Several cardiovascular risk factors cause no symptoms for a long time. Knowing your blood pressure, blood glucose and blood lipids therefore provides a better basis for assessing your personal risk.
Your baseline values, including blood pressure, blood glucose and blood lipids, and the resulting personal 10-year risk.
Important preparation for the appointment: ask whether ApoB provides additional information for your risk profile and whether Lp(a) has already been measured once.
Weight in the underweight range
Underweight is rarely questioned, but it can involve nutrient deficiency, muscle loss and bone density and may have a treatable cause.
The causes, nutrient supply and whether nutritional counselling would be useful.
Stopping smoking – one of your most powerful levers

Stopping smoking is one of the most powerful controllable health levers. After about one year, the risk of coronary heart disease is approximately half that of someone who continues to smoke; after around 15 years, it approaches the risk of someone who has never smoked. E-cigarettes and shisha are not harmless either.
Set a stop date within the next 14 days and call the free stop-smoking helpline on 0848 000 181. Guidance combined with nicotine replacement multiplies the chance of success.

What makes the difference: relapse is the rule rather than the exception, and several attempts are needed on average. The key is not never to fail but to restart quickly after a relapse. Nicotine replacement eases physical withdrawal, while guidance supports behaviour change.
Reduce alcohol

There is no risk-free level of alcohol consumption for cancer risk: even small amounts increase the risk of certain cancers. Overall, the less alcohol you drink, the lower the health burden. Quantity and heavy drinking on individual occasions are also relevant.
Set three fixed alcohol-free days this week. Choose specific days in your calendar rather than simply intending to drink less.
Body composition and metabolism
Waist circumference and BMI describe different aspects of body composition and complement each other when assessing metabolic and cardiovascular risk. Both values are guides, not a diagnosis.

After breathing out normally, measure approximately halfway between your lowest palpable rib and the top of your hip bone. As a rough guide, a waist circumference of less than half your height can be used.

You have already entered your waist circumference. Record the value to track it over time and include it together with weight, blood pressure, blood glucose and blood lipids in a professional risk assessment.
Physical activity – starting makes the greatest difference

Even additional physical activity below the recommended weekly target is associated with health benefits. Studies show a strong association between cardiorespiratory fitness, health and life expectancy.
Walk briskly for 10–15 minutes three times this week. Use the talk test: conversation is possible, singing is not.

Short bursts of vigorous everyday activity can complement fitness. Observational studies associate a few one- to two-minute peaks of activity with lower cardiovascular risk; this does not yet establish an individual causal effect. Start at a level suited to your capacity.
No strength training
Muscle mass and strength tend to decline with age without a regular training stimulus. Strength training on at least two days per week helps maintain or improve strength and function.
Twice a week, do 20 minutes of squats, push-ups and lunges, without equipment or a gym.
Break up long periods of sitting

Both total sitting time and long uninterrupted periods of sitting are relevant. Standing up regularly and taking short walking breaks add movement to the day, while sufficient overall physical activity remains important.
A practical mini-action: stand up, stretch or walk a few steps regularly, for example using a reminder. A short walk after eating can also slow the rise in blood glucose.
Uncertainty during everyday movements

Feeling unsteady often precedes a first fall by years and is therefore a valuable early warning sign. Balance is not a talent but a trainable ability, and measurable progress can appear within a few weeks.
Stand on one leg while brushing your teeth, for 20–30 seconds per side, with light support.
Mobility and balance

How easily you can get up without using your hands and maintain your balance provides a practical indication of strength, mobility and functional independence. It does not replace a medical examination.
Get up from a chair without using your hands five times each day. This trains leg strength and the mechanics of standing up at the same time.
Sleep that is not very restorative

Alcohol can make it easier to fall asleep, but it often fragments sleep and particularly reduces REM sleep. People metabolise caffeine at different rates, and late caffeine can still affect sleep hours later.
Keep your wake time as consistent as possible, including at weekends, and seek daylight soon after getting up. Both support a regular sleep–wake rhythm.
Social media takes up a lot of space

The apps are designed to hold your attention. Finding it difficult to stop is a result of product design, not a lack of willpower. Measures that increase the barrier are therefore more effective than good intentions.
Charge your phone outside the bedroom overnight and remove the two most time-consuming apps from your home screen.
Sugar and highly processed foods

Sugar-sweetened beverages are usually much less filling than solid foods. Depending on the product, half a litre of soft drink can contain around 50 g of sugar, so water or an unsweetened option is a manageable replacement.
Replace one sugary drink per day with water. Pure fruit juice also counts.

Also consider the combination: liquid sugar and highly processed products reinforce each other because both provide a lot of energy and only brief satiety. The plan therefore begins with the easiest daily swap.
Noticeable pressure in daily life
Recovery does not happen in whatever spare time remains; it must be planned like an appointment. Even a few minutes of deliberate rest measurably reduce the stress response.
Block two fixed 10-minute breaks per day in your calendar, without screens.
Limited social connection
Social connection is one of the strongest known protective factors for health and life expectancy, comparable with established lifestyle factors. Yet it is rarely maintained deliberately.
Actively contact one person this week and arrange something specific rather than vaguely intending to meet again.
Possible causes or gaps in nutrient supply can be identified and treated specifically if necessary.
You can track changes over time and decide together with a healthcare professional which further measurements or changes are appropriate.

Push-up test

The test primarily reflects the muscular endurance of the chest, shoulders, arms and core. Muscular strength supports resilience, mobility and healthy ageing. The result is a training guide, not a cardiovascular risk test.
Your result shows your current performance using the variation you selected. Until the protocol and reference table correspond unambiguously, we deliberately do not show a reference category.

The wall sit shows the local static muscular endurance of your leg muscles. This supports standing up, climbing stairs and stable everyday movement. The test does not measure your cardiovascular endurance.
